The great-souled one from whom all beings are born and into whom they will dissolve — who is able to praise him?
vishnupurana:55:13	Yet we, whose valour has been crushed by the destruction wrought by our enemies, seeking prosperity, shall praise you, though the true meaning of your words is beyond our reach.
vishnupurana:55:14	You are earth, water, fire, wind and space, the whole inner organ, pradhana, and the Person beyond it.
vishnupurana:55:15	This is your one body, self of beings, consisting of form and the formless, from Brahma down to a clump of grass, differentiated by place and time.
vishnupurana:55:16	Lord, your first form, born from the lotus of your navel for the sake of creation — salutation to you in the form of Brahma.
vishnupurana:55:17	We ourselves, differentiated as Shakra, the Sun, Rudra, the Vasus, the Ashvins, the Maruts, Soma and the rest, are your form — salutation to you in the form of the gods.
vishnupurana:55:18	Your form, Govinda, that is full of pride, unenlightened, lacking forbearance and self-control — salutation to you in the form of the daityas.
vishnupurana:55:19	That in which the channels do not carry great knowledge, whose radiance is dimmed, which is greedy for sound and the other objects — salutation to you in the form of the yakshas.
vishnupurana:55:20	Your dark, dreadful form, full of cruelty and deceit — salutation to you in the form of the night-rovers, Supreme Person.
vishnupurana:55:21	Your form called Dharma, the means to the fruit of the good dharma of the righteous dwelling in heaven — salutation to it, Janardana.
vishnupurana:55:22	Your form, perfected one, full of joy, unattached, moving freely in going and the like — salutation to you in the form of the siddhas.
vishnupurana:55:23	Your form, Hari, rich in impatience, cruel, capable of enjoyment, double-tongued — salutation to you in the form of the serpents.
vishnupurana:55:24	That which is enlightened, tranquil, faultless and free of stain — salutation to that form of yours, Vishnu, in the form of the sages.
vishnupurana:55:25	Your form, lotus-eyed one, that irresistibly devours beings at the end of the kalpa — salutation to you in the form of Time.
vishnupurana:55:26	The form that, having devoured all beings, gods and the rest without distinction, dances at the end — salutation to you in the form of Rudra.
vishnupurana:55:27	That which, through the working of rajas, is the cause of actions — salutation, Janardana, to that form of yours in the form of man.
vishnupurana:55:28	Your tamasic form, subject to the twenty-eight defects, going astray, self of all — salutation to you in the form of beasts.
vishnupurana:55:29	The form that is part of sacrifice, the means to the world's accomplishment, divided into trees and the rest — salutation to you in the form of the principal creation.
vishnupurana:55:30	Your form, first of all, which is animals, men, gods and the rest, space, sound and the rest — salutation to you, self of all.
vishnupurana:55:31	Supreme self, your first, supreme form, other than all this consisting of pradhana, intellect and the rest, and equal to nothing else — salutation to it, cause of causes.
vishnupurana:55:32	To that form, Blessed One, free of white and other colours, of length and the like, of density and the like, beyond the reach of epithets, purer than the pure, seen by the supreme sages — we bow.
vishnupurana:55:33	That which is unborn and imperishable in our bodies, in other bodies and in all things, apart from which nothing else exists — to that form of Brahman we bow.
vishnupurana:55:34	This whole world is the form of the unborn, eternal one whose self is the supreme state; to him, the undying, the seed of all, the stainless lord Vasudeva, we bow.
At the end of this hymn the gods saw the supreme Lord Hari, conch, discus and mace in hand, seated on Garuda.
All the gods, bowing first, said to him, seeking refuge: "Be gracious, god; protect us from the daityas.
The three worlds and our shares of sacrifice have been seized by the daityas headed by Hrada, transgressing even Brahma's command, supreme Lord.
Though we and they are both portions of you, who are all beings, still through the division of ignorance we see the world as divided.
Devoted to the dharma of their own castes, following the Vedic path and endowed with austerity, those enemies cannot be slain by us.
Self of all, you should give us the means by which we may be able to slay those asuras, Blessed One."
Thus addressed, the blessed Vishnu produced Mayamoha from his body, gave him to them and said to the best of the gods:

This Mayamoha will delude all those daityas; then, excluded from the Vedic path, they will be slayable.
vishnupurana:55:43	For all adversaries of Brahma's authority, gods, daityas and others, are to be slain by me who abide in preservation.
vishnupurana:55:44	So go, and have no fear; let this Mayamoha go before you today; he will be of help to you, gods.
Thus addressed, the gods bowed to him and went back as they had come, and Mayamoha went with them to where the great asuras were.
Others too, brahmin, Mayamoha, the great deluder, deluded by many other kinds of heresy.
In a very short time those asuras, deluded by Mayamoha, abandoned all discourse based on the path of the three Vedas.
Some reviled the Vedas, others the gods, brahmin, others the whole range of sacrificial rites, and others the twice-born:

This statement does not stand reason: violence is not accepted as dharma; that oblations burned in fire bring fruit is the talk of children.
vishnupurana:56:27	If Indra, having attained godhood by many sacrifices, eats shami wood and the like, then a leaf-eating beast is better... [the rest of this verse is corrupt in the source] …
vishnupurana:56:28	If a beast slain in sacrifice is held to attain heaven, why does the sacrificer not slay his own father?
vishnupurana:56:29	If what is eaten by one person gives satisfaction to another, then one should give shraddha food with faith, and travellers need not carry provisions.
vishnupurana:56:30	Understanding that this is merely what people believe, indifference to it is better for you; let what I have said please you.
vishnupurana:56:31	Authoritative statements do not fall from the sky, great asuras; reasoned words are to be accepted, by me and by others like you.
Thus the daityas were turned away by Mayamoha in many ways, so that none of them cared for the three Vedas.
When the daityas had thus gone astray, the immortals made supreme effort and came forward for battle.
Then a battle of gods and asuras took place again, brahmin, and the asuras, adversaries of the good path, were slain by the gods.
The armour of true dharma which they had at first, brahmin, had protected them before; when it was lost, they perished.

Then, Maitreya, the people who followed their path became the "naked," since they had abandoned the covering of the three Vedas; and those asuras, revilers of the various Vedas, were made powerless by the gods.
The celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the wandering ascetic — these are the four ashramas; a fifth is not admitted.
Whoever gives up household life and does not become a forest-dweller or a wandering ascetic, Maitreya, is a naked man, a doer of sin.
Brahmin, he loses the obligatory rites day and night; not doing the prescribed rite though able, he falls on that very day.
A man who neglects the daily rites for a fortnight, Maitreya, attains purity only by a great penance, when not in distress.
The man whose rites have lapsed for a year — on seeing him, the good should always look at the sun.
If touched by him, bathing with one's clothes on is the means of purification, great sage; but for that sinner himself no purification is declared.
The man from whose house the gods, sages, ancestors and beings depart unhonoured, sighing — there is no greater sinner than he.
With one whose body and house are struck by the sighs of the gods and others, one should not mix by sharing house, seat or belongings.
One who converses with him, questions him and laughs with him becomes equal to him for a year, brahmin.
And one who eats in his house, sits on the same seat or lies on the same bed becomes at once equal to him.
Whoever eats without honouring the gods, ancestors, beings and guests eats sin; what expiation is there for him?
Brahmins and the other castes who turn away from their own dharma, abiding in low occupations, get the name "naked."
Where there is utter mixture of the four castes, Maitreya, staying there leads to the ruin of those of good conduct.
By conversing with one who eats without honouring the sages, gods, ancestors, beings and guests, men fall into hell.
Therefore a wise man should always avoid these naked ones, tainted by abandoning the three Vedas, in speech, touch and the like.
A shraddha made with effort by the faithful does not please the gods, fathers and grandfathers if these have looked upon it.
It is heard that long ago there was a famous king on earth, Shatadhanu, and his wife Shaibya, exceedingly devoted to dharma,
devoted to her husband, most fortunate, endowed with truth, purity and compassion, possessed of every good mark and of modesty.
That king with her worshipped the god of gods, Janardana, the all-pervading, with supreme concentration,
with oblations, japa, gifts and fasts with devotion, and with worship day by day, his mind on him and on nothing else.
Once, having bathed together in the water of the Bhagirathi on the full moon of Kartika after fasting, husband and wife came out and saw a heretic coming toward them, brahmin.
He was a friend of the great-souled king's teacher of archery; so, out of regard for him, the king conversed with him.
But the queen, his wife of restrained vows, kept silent: "I have fasted," she thought, and on seeing him she looked at the sun.
Coming home, the couple duly performed all the worship of Vishnu and the rest according to rule, best of the twice-born.
As time went on, the king, conqueror of his enemies, died, and the queen ascended the pyre after her husband, the king.
Because of that fault — the conversation with a heretic while fasting — the lord of the earth was born a dog.
She was born the lovely daughter of the king of Kashi, remembering her former birth, endowed with all knowledge and adorned with every good mark.
Her father wished to give her to a suitor, but was stopped by the slender girl herself, and the king desisted from arranging the marriage.
Then, seeing with divine sight that her husband had become a dog, she went to the city called Vaidisha and saw him in that state.
Seeing her husband become a dog, the fortunate one gave him excellent food, full of honour and kindness.
Eating the most tasty and desired food she gave him, he fawned on her greatly with the playful ways of dogs.
The girl, greatly ashamed at his fawning, bowed and said this to her beloved born in a low womb:

Remember, great king, that courtesy of yours by which you have fallen into the womb of a dog and fawn upon me.
vishnupurana:56:70	Having spoken with a heretic after bathing at a holy place, you have reached a contemptible birth; do you not remember it, lord?
Reminded thus of what happened in his former birth, he pondered long and then attained a detachment most hard to gain.
With a mind grown weary of the world, he went out of the city, threw himself from a cliff in the desert and was born as a jackal.
When the next year came, she, knowing by divine sight that he was a jackal, went to Mount Kolahala to see him.
There too, seeing her husband come into a jackal's birth, the lovely daughter of the king said to him:
Do you remember, king of kings, what I told you when you were in a dog's birth about your former conduct, based on conversing with a heretic?
Knowing again what she said to be true, the best of the truthful gave up his body in the forest without food.
Then, when he was born again as a wolf, the blameless one went to him in a lonely forest and reminded her husband of what had happened before:
You are not a wolf, fortunate one; you are King Shatadhanu; having been a dog, you became a jackal, and now you have become a wolf.
Reminded thus, he abandoned that body and became a vulture; and the sinless lady again awakened him:
Lord of men, remember yourself; enough of a vulture's ways. This fault, by which you have become a vulture, arose from conversing with a heretic.
Then, when in the next birth he had become a crow, the slender one, finding her husband by her yoga, said:
You, to whom all kings were formerly subject and gave tribute, have now become a crow, an eater of offerings, lord.
Reminded thus of the past in his birth as a crow, the lord of the earth gave up his life and became a peacock.
When he was a peacock, the good girl kept him near her, giving him every moment food fit for his kind.
Then King Janaka performed the great horse sacrifice, and at its concluding bath she had him bathed;
the slender one bathed herself too and reminded him how the king had taken the births of dog, jackal and the rest.
Remembering the sequence of his births, he then gave up his body and was born as the son of that same great-souled Janaka.
Then the slender one urged her father to arrange her marriage, and her father held a self-choice ceremony for her.
When the self-choice was held, the lady chose him who had come, her own husband, again as her husband.
The prince enjoyed pleasures with her, and when his father died he ruled the kingdom among the Videhas.
He performed many sacrifices, gave gifts to the needy, begot sons and fought with his enemies.
Having ruled the kingdom justly and protected the earth, the king gave up his dear life in battle according to dharma.
Then the fair-eyed one, joyful, again ascended the pyre after her husband according to rule, as before.
Then that king, together with the princess, passing beyond the worlds of Indra, attained imperishable worlds that yield every desire.
They obtained the incomparable imperishability of heaven, a married union most rare, the fruit of merit, and that purification, best of the twice-born.
This fault of conversing with heretics has been told by me, brahmin, and likewise the greatness of the concluding bath of the horse sacrifice.
Therefore one should avoid conversation and contact with sinful heretics, especially at the time of rites and when consecrated for a sacrifice and the like.
On seeing one in whose house the rites have lapsed for a single month, a wise man should look at the sun.

How much more, brahmin, with those who have wholly abandoned the three Vedas, sinners who eat others' food and oppose the teachings of the Veda! Conversation, association and sitting together with heretics of evil conduct is most sinful; therefore one should avoid them.

One should not honour, even by a word, heretics, those in forbidden occupations, those who keep the cat's vow, deceivers, sophists and those who live like herons. The heretic has fallen from his own dharma; one in forbidden occupations does what is prohibited. One who always raises his dharma like a banner while his sins are hidden — that is the vow called the cat's. One who speaks pleasantly to one's face but does great harm elsewhere, and whose acts are offences, is called a deceiver by the wise. One who raises doubts about good works through arguments is a sophist. Those of short-sighted vision, dishonest, intent on their own gain, deceitful and falsely humble are called heron-like.
Association and even sitting together with sinful heretics of evil conduct should be avoided from afar; therefore one should avoid them.
These naked ones have been described to you, who spoil a shraddha by their glance; by conversing with them men's merit for the day perishes.
These heretics are sinners; the wise should not converse with them; by conversing with them the merit arising that day is destroyed.

By even conversing with men who uselessly wear matted hair or shave their heads, who eat in vain, who have rejected all purity and are excluded from offerings of water and pindas to the ancestors, men go to hell.
When it was said, "So it shall be," from the southern fire there arose a great kritya, because he had placed the fire there.
Then the kritya, her mouth terrible with flames and her mass of hair blazing, crying "Krishna, Krishna!" in anger, went to Dvaravati.
Seeing her, the people, their eyes darting with terror, went to Madhusudana, refuge of the worlds, for refuge, sage.
The discus-bearer, understanding that this great kritya had been produced by the son of the king of Kashi after worshipping the bull-bannered god,
said, "Slay this fierce kritya, her matted hair a mass of fiery flames," and, absorbed in playing at dice, playfully released his discus.
Vishnu's discus Sudarshana quickly pursued the kritya, most terrible with her matted locks of garlanded fire and her spewing flames.
Shattered by the might of the discus, the kritya of Maheshvara then fled swiftly, and it pursued her with speed.
The kritya, her power checked by Vishnu's discus, hurriedly entered Varanasi itself, best of sages.
Then the great army of Kashi and likewise the army of the pramathas, equipped with every weapon and missile, went out against the discus.
Having burned by its might that army skilled in discharging weapons, Hari's discus then burned the whole city of Varanasi, which had borne the kritya,
with its king, servants and citizens, with its horses, elephants and men, with all its treasuries and granaries, hard to look upon even for the gods,
all its houses, walls and squares wreathed in flames — it burned the entire city.
Its wrath undiminished, eager for more though little remained to be done, that discus of Vishnu, flashing with brilliance, returned to his hand.
Then Baladeva went to the city named after the elephant and stayed in the middle of an outer garden, not entering the city.
Learning that Bala had come, the kings Duryodhana and the others offered Rama a cow, guest-water and water.
Having duly accepted all this, he said to the Kauravas: "Ugrasena commands: release Samba at once."
Hearing these words, Bhishma, Drona and the others, brahmin, Karna, Duryodhana and the rest grew angry, best of the twice-born.
All the Kauravas, Bahlika and the others, spoke in anger, regarding the line of Yadu as unfit for kingship, to the club-armed one:

Ho, what is this speech you have uttered, Balabhadra? What Yadava shall give commands to those born of the Kuru line?
vishnupurana:115:14	If even Ugrasena is to give commands to the Kauravas, then enough of these white umbrellas fit for kings, which are made a mockery.
vishnupurana:115:15	So go, Bala, or not; we shall not release Samba, who acted unjustly, at your command or Ugrasena's.
vishnupurana:115:16	The obeisance that the Kukuras and Andhakas made to us, who are to be honoured, they have made; what is this command from servant to master?
vishnupurana:115:17	You have been made proud by sharing seats and meals with us; what fault is ours, that policy was not observed out of affection?
vishnupurana:115:18	This guest-offering we presented to you, Bala, was out of love; it is not what befits your family from ours.
Having said this, all the Kurus, firmly resolved, "We shall not release Hari's son," quickly entered the elephant city.
Then, intoxicated and reeling with anger born of the insult, the plough-armed one rose and struck the earth with his heel.
The earth was split by the heel-blow of the great-souled one; he clapped his arms, filling the quarters with the sound,
and spoke, his eyes deep red, his face twisted with frowning brows:

Oh, this arrogance of intoxication of the worthless, wicked Kauravas! Our sovereignty, it seems, is a matter of time, since they still regard Ugrasena's command as something to be transgressed.
vishnupurana:115:24	The lord of Shachi, with the gods, should accept his command in accordance with dharma; ... Ugrasena presides over Sudharma, not the lord of Shachi.
vishnupurana:115:25	Fie on their satisfaction with a royal seat left over by a hundred men! He whose servants' wives wear clusters of flowers of the Parijata tree — is even he not their king?
vishnupurana:115:26	Let Ugrasena stand as lord of all kings; today I shall rid the earth of the Kauravas and go to his city.
vishnupurana:115:27	Karna, Duryodhana, Drona, Bhishma with Bahlika, Duhshasana and the rest, Bhuri and Bhurishravas,
vishnupurana:115:28	Somadatta, Shala, Bhima, Arjuna with Yudhishthira, the twins and the other Kauravas — slaying them with their horses, chariots and elephants,
vishnupurana:115:29	and taking the hero Samba with his wife, I shall go to the city of Dvaraka and see Ugrasena and my other kinsmen.
vishnupurana:115:30	Or, urged by the king of the gods to relieve the earth's burden quickly, I shall at once cast the Kaurava capital, the city named after the elephant, with all the Kurus into the Bhagirathi.
Having said this, his eyes red with intoxication, the club-armed one set his plough point-downward against the rampart and dragged it.
Seeing Hastinapura suddenly shaken, all the Kauravas cried out with agitated hearts:

Rama, Rama, mighty-armed one, forgive, forgive! Withdraw your anger; be gracious, club-armed one.
vishnupurana:115:34	Here is Samba with his wife, handed over to you, Bala; forgive us offenders who did not know your power.
Then the Kauravas quickly came out of their city and handed over Samba together with his wife, bull among sages.
To Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and the others, who bowed and spoke kindly, Bala, best of the strong, said, "I have forgiven."
Even today that city is seen with a tilted shape, brahmin; such is the power of Rama, marked by strength and valour.
Then the Kauravas, having honoured Samba, sent him with the plough-bearer, together with wedding wealth and his wife.
Then, deluded by ignorance, he destroyed sacrifices, broke the bounds of the good and brought destruction on embodied beings.
The fickle one burned lands, cities and villages; sometimes he crushed villages and the like by hurling mountains.
Uprooting mountains, he flung them into the waters and the ocean; and again, standing in the midst of the ocean, he agitated the sea.
Agitated by him, the ocean overflowed its shores, brahmin, flooding with great force the villages, cities and the like on its banks.
The monkey, able to take any form, assumed a huge form and crushed all the crops, rolling, roaming and trampling.
By that wicked one this whole world was wronged; without Vedic recitation and the vashat call, Maitreya, it was in great distress.
Once, in the Raivata garden, the plough-armed one was drinking liquor, with the fortunate Revati and other lovely women.
Sung to, amid the heads of sporting women, the best of the Yadus was enjoying himself like Kubera on the Mandara.
Then that monkey came, seized the plough-bearer's plough and club, and mimicked him to his face.
Likewise the monkey laughed in the faces of those women, and kicking with his foot he knocked over the cups full of liquor.
Then Bala, filled with anger, rebuked him; yet the monkey, scorning him, made a chattering noise.
Then Bala rose and seized his club in wrath, and the best of monkeys seized a dreadful mountain rock.
He hurled it, and the best of the Yadavas shattered it into a thousand pieces with his club as it came, and it fell to the ground.
Leaping over the descending club, the monkey came with speed and struck him on the chest with his palm in rage.
Then, struck on the head by Bala's fist in anger, Dvivida fell vomiting blood, his life ended.
By the fall of his body the mountain peak was shattered into a hundred pieces, Maitreya, as if struck by the thunderbolt of the thunderbolt-wielder.
Then the gods rained flowers on Rama and came and praised him: "Well done! This is a great deed of yours.
By this wicked monkey, who helped the daityas' side, the world was harassed, hero; fortunately he has met his end." Having said this, the gods went to heaven delighted, with the guhyakas.
Such are the many immeasurable deeds of the wise Baladeva, Shesha, the upholder of the earth.

As they drank there, through friction with one another a fire of strife arose, fuelled by abusive words, bringing destruction. [Maitreya asked:] "As each was eating his own, how did the quarrel or friction arise without cause, best of brahmins? You should tell me." [Parashara said:] As they said, "My food is tasty, yours is not," a dispute about tasty and untasty arose, then friction and strife; and then, rushing at one another, their eyes red with anger,
they struck each other with weapons, compelled by the power of fate; when their weapons were exhausted they seized the eraka reeds growing nearby.
The eraka grass seized by them looked like thunderbolts; with it they struck each other in a most dreadful fight.
Pradyumna, Samba and the others, Kritavarman and Satyaki, Aniruddha and the rest, Prithu and Viprithu,
Charuvarman, Charuka and Akrura and the others, brahmin, struck each other with thunderbolts in the form of eraka reeds.
Hari tried to stop the Yadavas, but they thought Keshava had come as an ally of their opponents, and struck each other.
Krishna too, angered, took a handful of eraka to slay them, and that handful became an iron club.
With it he slew all the murderous Yadavas, and the others too, rushing suddenly, struck each other.
Then, as Daruka watched, the victorious chariot of the discus-bearer was quickly carried off by the horses across the midst of the ocean, best of the twice-born.
The discus, the mace, the Sharnga bow, the quivers, the conch and the sword circumambulated Hari and went by the path of the sun.
In a moment there was no Yadava left unslain except mighty-armed Krishna and Daruka, great sage.
Walking about, the two saw Rama seated at the foot of a tree, and a great serpent coming out of his mouth.
Having come out of his mouth, the serpent of great coils went to the ocean, worshipped by siddhas and serpents.
Then the ocean, taking a guest-offering, came before him, and he entered its waters, worshipped by the best of serpents.
Seeing Bala's departure, Keshava said to Daruka: "Tell all this to Vasudeva and Ugrasena —
the departure of Balabhadra and the destruction of the Yadavas; I too, abiding in yoga, shall give up this body.
And tell all the people dwelling in Dvaraka, and Ahuka, that the ocean will flood this whole city.
Therefore, being ready, you should await the coming of Arjuna; do not stay in Dvaraka once the Pandava has left;
you should go with him wherever that Kaurava goes.
And go and tell Arjuna, son of Kunti, in my words: 'These people, my dependants, are to be protected by you according to your strength.'
So take the people of Dvaravati and go with Arjuna, and Vajra shall be king of the Yadus."
Thus addressed, Daruka bowed to Krishna again and again, circumambulated him many times and went as instructed.
Having gone, the wise one did so in Dvaraka, brought Arjuna, and made Vajra king.

The blessed Govinda too, placing the supreme Brahman consisting of Vasudeva in himself, held it in all beings; uniting himself, fortunate one, with the self beyond the manifold, the Supreme Person lay in the fourth state, as in play.
Honouring the brahmin's words that Durvasas had spoken, he sat absorbed in yoga, placing his foot on his knee, best of beings.
Then a hunter named Jara came there, having set as the head of his lance an arrow made from the iron remnant of the club.
Seeing from a distance that foot shaped like a deer, he pierced its sole with that very lance, best of the twice-born.
Going there, he saw a man bearing four arms; he bowed and said to him again and again, "Be gracious!
I did this unknowingly, taking you for a deer; forgive me; you should not burn me, already burned by my own sin."
Then the Blessed One said to him: "You have not the least fear; go, hunter, by my grace, to heaven, the abode of the gods."
Immediately after his words an aerial car came, and mounting it the hunter went to heaven by his grace.
When he had gone, the Blessed One, uniting himself with the self — Brahman, imperishable, inconceivable, consisting of Vasudeva, stainless,
unborn, unaging, undying, immeasurable, the self of all — gave up his human body, passing beyond the threefold course.

Having slain Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha, Karna and the rest, he has grown proud and does not know the strength of village dwellers.
vishnupurana:118:17	Ho, take up your long staves! This fool despises us all; what are your raised arms for?
Then robbers armed with staves, plunderers of booty, rushed by the thousands at those people whose master had been slain.
Then the son of Kunti turned back and said to the Abhiras, as if laughing: "Turn back, you who know not dharma, if you do not wish to die."
Scorning his words, they then seized the wealth and the women, Maitreya, the dependants of Vishvaksena.
Then Arjuna began to string his divine bow Gandiva, never failing in battle, but the mighty one could not.
He strung it with difficulty, and it became slack again; nor could the Pandava remember his divine weapons, though he tried.
The son of Pritha, enraged, shot arrows at these enemies, but shot by the wielder of Gandiva they only pierced the skin.
The inexhaustible arrows given by Agni were exhausted as Arjuna fought with the cowherds at the end of his prosperity.
And the son of Kunti reflected: "It was Krishna's strength alone by which I conquered all kings with volleys of arrows."
Then, while the son of Pandu looked on, those best of women were dragged away by the Abhiras, and others went willingly.
Then, when his arrows were spent, Dhananjaya struck the robbers with the tip of his bow, and they laughed at his blows, sage.
And while the son of Pritha watched, those mlecchas went off taking all the fine women of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, best of sages.
Then Jishnu, greatly distressed, saying "Alas, alas!", wept: "Oh, I have been abandoned by the Blessed One!
That bow, those weapons, that chariot and those horses — all perished at a stroke, like a gift given to one ignorant of the Veda.
Oh, fate is exceedingly strong, since without that great-souled one it gives victory to the lowly and incapable.
These are the same arms, the same fist, the same place, and I am the same Arjuna; yet without that holy one all has become worthless.
Surely my Arjuna-hood and Bhima's Bhima-hood were his doing; without him, how else could I have been conquered by the Abhiras?"
Speaking thus, Jishnu went to the excellent city called Mathura, and there made Vajra, delight of the Yadavas, king.
Then Phalguna saw Vyasa dwelling in the forest; approaching the fortunate one, he saluted him with humility.
Looking long at him as he saluted his feet, the sage said to the son of Pritha: "Why are you so utterly without lustre?

Have you followed an unworthy woman, or killed a brahmin? You look bereft of lustre like one grieving at the breaking of a firm hope. Or did you fail to give in the month of Urja and in the dark fortnight, or give discoloured food mixed with wheat, without bowing to Vishnu, the giver of all desires — is that why your form appears thus?
Or were those begging for the sake of offspring and the like turned away by you, or did you delight in a woman you should not approach, that you are without radiance?
Do you eat something sweet alone without giving to brahmins, or did you take the wealth of the poor, Arjuna?
Have you come within the wind of a winnowing basket, Arjuna, or been struck by the evil eye? How else are you without glory?
Or were you touched by water from someone's nails, or sprinkled with water from a pot, that you are so without lustre, or were you defeated in battle by inferiors?"
Then the son of Pritha sighed, and told by him, "Listen, Blessed One," he related to Vyasa his humiliation as it had happened:

Our strength, our radiance, our valour, our prowess, our glory and our splendour — Hari, abandoning us, has gone.

Rambha, Tilottama and the other apsarases known to the Veda said to him: "When you are pleased, what is lacking to us, brahmin?"
But the others said: "If the blessed one is pleased, we wish to obtain the Supreme Person as our husband, chief of brahmins."

Thus addressed, Arjuna came to the two sons of Pritha and the twins, and told them in detail what he had seen and experienced.
All of them, hearing Vyasa's words as Arjuna reported them, placed Parikshit on the throne, and the sons of Pandu went to the forest.
Thus I have told you at length, Maitreya, the deeds of Vasudeva born in the line of Yadu; whoever always hears this story of Krishna is freed from all sins and goes to Vishnu's world.
The special movement of the mind, dependent on one's own effort, and its union with Brahman — that is called yoga.

He whose yoga is marked by such a dharma of utmost distinction is called a yogi, one seeking liberation. There is only one cause of bondage and liberation, no second; the path to the eastern ocean does not lead to the western. The understanding does not arise from attachment by action in a former birth; thus dharma through its means is not a cause in other dharmas.
The yogi joined to yoga at first is called the practitioner; but one whose samadhi is perfected has realized the supreme Brahman.
If his mind is spoiled by the fault of some obstacle, then for the former, practising through further births, liberation arises.
But the yogi whose samadhi is perfected attains liberation in that very birth, the mass of his karma soon burned by the fire of yoga.
The yogi, free of desire, bringing his mind to fitness, should practise celibacy, non-violence, truth, non-stealing and non-possession.
With self-restraint he should practise Vedic study, purity, contentment and austerity, and turn his mind toward the supreme Brahman.
These five yamas and five niyamas are declared; practised with desire they give special fruits, and for the desireless they give liberation.
Taking one of the postures such as bhadrasana, endowed with the qualities called yamas and niyamas, the restrained ascetic should practise yoga.
Bringing under control by practice the wind called prana — that is to be known as pranayama, with seed and without seed.
